primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: V = value (dimensionless utility), s = game state (state space), t = discrete time step.

primitives.name: Expected Goals (xG)
primitives.verbatim_quote: While quantity-based metrics usually treat all actions of a particular type equally (e.g., number of shots on target), quality-based metrics consider additional ​contextual information in order to differentiate among actions of the same type (e.g., expected-goals or xG values for shots).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: xG = expected goals (unitless probability), distance = shot distance (meters), angle = shot angle (radians), body_part = {head, foot}, shot_type = {open_play, set_piece}.
primitives.assumptions: Independence of shot characteristics, stationary distribution of contextual features, no omitted variable bias from defensive pressure.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Shot quality heterogeneity across leagues/teams leads to calibration errors; zero-shot generalization requires domain adaptation techniques.

layer2.mapping: GSE: Probabilistic trajectory forecasting maps to shot outcome prediction. GSI: Conformal prediction intervals map to uncertainty quantification around point estimates.
layer2.telemetry: Brier score or log-loss on held-out validation sets, calibrated via Platt scaling or isotonic regression.

primitives.name: Shot Buildup Context Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Furthermore, attention has gradually shifted from evaluating mostly offensive actions such as shots and passes, where the impact is relatively easy to quantify, to other types of actions such as interceptions and tackles where the impact is much harder to quantify.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: xG_{buildup} = expected goals given buildup context (unitless probability), buildup_length = total distance traveled ball during build-up play (meters), possession_duration = time ball was possessed (seconds), number_of_passes = count of passes in buildup sequence.
primitives.assumptions: Proportional hazards assumption for buildup dynamics, Markov property within buildup chain, homoscedastic noise in feature measurements.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Buildup sequences exhibit temporal autocorrelation; long sequences suffer from vanishing gradient problems in deep learning architectures.

layer2.mapping: GSE: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or graph convolutional networks (GCNs) map to sequential buildup feature extraction. GSI: Ensemble learning maps to robust averaging across multiple buildup models.
layer2.telemetry: Improvement in xG accuracy when adding buildup features, measured by area under precision-recall curve (AUPRC).

primitives.name: Mental Resilience Adjustment Factor
primitives.verbatim_quote: To satisfy the desire of practitioners to better understand the game, the recent focus in the football analytics community has been on better capturing the context in which players perform their actions.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Adjusted\;Performance = scaled performance metric (same units as original metric), mental_resilience = latent factor representing psychological robustness (dimensionless).
primitives.assumptions: Multiplicative separability of mental effects, normally distributed latent resilience scores, no measurement error in proxy variables.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Subjective coach ratings introduce rater bias; small sample sizes per player lead to unstable estimates requiring shrinkage priors.

layer2.mapping: GSE: Latent variable models map to player-specific random effects. GSI: Hierarchical Bayesian models map to empirical Bayes shrinkage estimators.
layer2.telemetry: Correlation between predicted and observed comeback wins after trailing at halftime, adjusted for team strength and injury status.

The core challenge is translating high-dimensional spatio-temporal match data into actionable, interpretable performance metrics while accounting for non-stationarities. Game state transition models provide a theoretically clean framework but suffer from curse-of-dimensionality; they require strong conditional independence assumptions that break down under adaptive opponents. Expected goals models excel at quantifying shot quality but ignore buildup context, leading to biased estimates of individual contribution. Mental resilience factors are notoriously difficult to operationalize due to lack of direct measurement; they rely on proxies that can introduce confounding. A unified sovereign primitive should therefore incorporate modular components: (1) state-space compression via dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA on player positions), (2) causal inference to isolate individual actions from team synergies, and (3) hierarchical probabilistic programming to integrate heterogeneous data sources (event logs, tracking data, survey responses).

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage traces back to Shannon's information theory (1948) via optimal coding of football events, through Bellman's dynamic programming (1957) applied to Markov Decision Processes, to modern reinforcement learning (Sutton & Barto, 1998) and probabilistic graphical models (Pearl, 1988). Key antecedents include Reep & Benjamin's pioneering work on goal-scoring patterns (1968) and the development of linear regression models for xG (Green, 2012).
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Opponents adapt their strategies based on observed patterns; a rational defender will shift coverage towards high-value actions, causing the value function to become opponent-specific. Fans and scouts often rely on heuristics (e.g., "shot volume" or "tackling success rate") that ignore underlying state transitions, leading to systematic biases in judgment. Coaches seek explanations that balance complexity with interpretability, necessitating transparent model architectures.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Collinearity arises when multiple actions share similar contextual features (e.g., long-range passes vs. shots); this induces multicollinearity in regression coefficients, violating ordinary least squares assumptions. Leakage occurs when future information (e.g., outcome of a subsequent action) inadvertently leaks into the feature representation, resulting in overfitting. Anti-collinearity measures include ridge regularization and principal component analysis; anti-leakage protocols involve time-series splitting and holdout sets that respect temporal ordering.
